pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–8 years

- **Topic:** Forces Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 3 Forces and Magnets; earlier informal at KS1):** Year 3 introduces forces vocabulary (forces needing contact vs magnetic forces acting at a distance); at 5–7 the words push and pull arise informally through play and exploration rather than as a statutory KS1 forces unit (forces are first statutory at Year 3).

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-PS2-1; DCI PS2.A):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1]; DCI PS2.A — '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1, K-PS2-2]' — underpins the early force vocabulary.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE topic: building a precise vocabulary for forces — force, push, pull, twist, stretch, squash, contact/non-contact, gravity, weight, friction, air resistance, upthrust — and using each word correctly to describe what is happening in a situation ('friction slows the sledge', 'gravity pulls the apple down'). The organising distinction is contact forces (need surfaces touching: push, pull, friction, upthrust, air resistance) versus non-contact forces (act at a distance: gravity, magnetism). Vocabulary is learned best when each word is anchored to a directly experienced phenomenon rather than memorised as a definition, taught explicitly (word + child-friendly meaning + examples and non-examples), and revisited across many contexts. 'Weight' is introduced as a force (the pull of gravity) and kept distinct from 'mass'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Introduce each term alongside the phenomenon it names — feel the stretch of an elastic band, the squash of dough, the twist of a lid — so the word labels a real experience.
Teach vocabulary explicitly: give a child-friendly meaning, several examples AND non-examples, and a sentence frame ('___ is the force that ___').
Use a contact vs non-contact sort as the central organiser; have children justify each placement ('does anything need to touch?').
Name the force acting in many varied scenarios (sledge, apple, boat, magnet) so words transfer across contexts; revisit/space the vocabulary rather than teaching it once.
Use word walls and labelled images of forces in action as a persistent reference.
Introduce 'weight' as a force (a pull) and flag that it is not the same as 'mass' — kept age-appropriate, since the full mass/weight quantification comes later.
keyRepresentations: Labelled images / word wall of forces in action (the canonical naming reference)
Tap-to-reveal annotated scenes (tap an interaction → force name + meaning + contact/non-contact tag)
Sentence frames matching a force word to a scenario
commonMisconceptions: Non-contact forces need contact or a medium — e.g. 'there's no gravity in space / on the Moon', or gravity 'needs air' to act.
Friction (or gravity) is a 'thing' or phenomenon, not named as a FORCE.
Believing only pushes and pulls count as forces, so gravity/friction/upthrust aren't recognised as forces.
Thinking water/air don't push — ignoring upthrust and air resistance as named forces.

learn.summary: Help 5–8 year-olds build and correctly use a precise vocabulary for forces (force, push, pull, twist, stretch, squash, contact/non-contact, gravity, weight, friction, air resistance, upthrust), anchoring each word to a directly experienced phenomenon and organising terms by whether something must be touching (contact) or whether the force acts across a gap (non-contact). This is a language-building topic; the aim is naming what is happening, not quantifying cause and effect. Weight is introduced as a force (the pull of gravity) and kept distinct from mass in age-appropriate terms.

activities.title: Forces all around us: name and tag the scene
feedback: If a learner expects the apple or the paperclip needs something touching to move: reveal that nothing is touching — gravity pulls the apple down, and the magnet pulls the paperclip across a gap, so these forces act at a distance — and set this next to the slide where friction clearly needs contact.
If a learner calls everything 'a push' or 'a force': model the specific word for that interaction (squash, stretch, pull, friction) and point to its picture example.
For the dropped apple, if 'gravity' or 'weight' is not offered: name gravity as the pull of the Earth, and weight as that pull.
For the boat, confirm both forces by name: upthrust pushes up, weight pulls down.
activities.rationale: Vocabulary sticks best when each word labels a real, observed phenomenon and is taught explicitly with meaning plus examples. A single rich scene lets many force words be anchored and the contact/non-contact organiser applied across varied cases, including the non-contact action-at-a-distance of gravity and magnetism. Interactive tap/lift-the-flap reveals are an optional way to stage the 'what's touching?' check; a labelled poster, picture cards, or a read-aloud walk through a real playground can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Gravitational, magnetic and electric effects are a special class of NON-CONTACT forces that act at a distance; the core pupil difficulty is discomfort with action-at-a-distance itself ('How can the Earth pull on the Moon to make it fall? It's not even touching it!'), and teachers are warned to keep magnetism and gravity separate as conflating them is a well-known difficulty. (Note: this is IOP 14-16 teaching guidance; the contact/non-contact framing transfers down, but the action-at-a-distance/field idea is developed later.)

K-PS2-1 asks students to '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1]'; DCI PS2.A: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1, K-PS2-2]. [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1, K-PS2-2].' This anchors the push/pull/strength/direction vocabulary.
learnerActions: Explore a rich, familiar scene full of forces in action — e.g. a child sliding down a slide (friction), a kicked ball (push), a dog on a lead (pull), a floating boat (upthrust), a falling apple (gravity), a stretched catapult (stretch), and a magnet pulling a paperclip across a gap (magnetism).
For each interaction, say or choose the correct force word and a one-line child-friendly meaning.
Ask of each one: 'Does anything need to touch for this force to act?' and tag it CONTACT or NON-CONTACT.

Compare the slide (friction clearly needs surfaces touching) with the falling apple (nothing touches it) and the magnet pulling a paperclip across a gap (the magnetic force acts without the magnet touching the paperclip), to notice the contrast between contact and non-contact forces.
Zoom into the floating boat to identify two forces at once: water pushing UP (upthrust) and weight pulling DOWN.
activities.intendedInsight: Each situation has a specific named force, and forces split into those that need things touching (pushes and pulls made by touching, such as a kick or a lead, plus friction, upthrust and air resistance) and those that act across a gap (gravity and magnetism, which are themselves pulls). The falling-apple and magnet-across-a-gap moments make the contact/non-contact distinction a felt contrast rather than a memorised definition.

activities.title: Feel the force, then name it
feedback: If a learner uses one general word for several different actions: do the actions again one at a time and model the distinct word for each.
If a learner picks a non-example as an example: contrast it directly with a true example and ask what is actually happening to the object.
activities.rationale: Introducing each term alongside the phenomenon it names, with child-friendly meaning, examples AND non-examples, and a sentence frame, supports explicit vocabulary instruction and first acquisition through direct experience.
learnerActions: Physically stretch an elastic band, squash a ball of dough, twist a jar lid, push a toy car, and pull a cart.
After each action, say the specific force word and complete a sentence frame: '___ is the force that ___' (e.g. 'A stretch is a pull that makes the band longer').
Sort a small set of example cards and non-example cards for each word (e.g. squashing dough IS a squash; pulling a cart is NOT a squash).
activities.intendedInsight: Force words name real experiences the learner can feel and produce, and each word has clear examples and non-examples that mark its boundary.

activities.title: Sort and label new examples (practice and retrieval)
feedback: For a mis-sort, revisit the 'does anything need to touch?' question for that specific card rather than giving the answer outright.
For 'which force slows the sledge?' confusions between gravity and friction: re-anchor friction as the rubbing force between surfaces touching, and gravity as the pull of the Earth.
activities.rationale: Active retrieval, sorting and matching with feedback consolidate vocabulary once it has been introduced; spacing and revisiting across varied contexts helps words transfer. These are consolidation tasks that follow, rather than replace, experience-anchored introduction.
learnerActions: Classify fresh scenario cards into CONTACT and NON-CONTACT groups, saying why ('does anything need to touch?').
Match each force word to the picture or scenario it describes.
Label a new scene by placing the correct force word onto each interaction.
Complete fill-in sentence frames such as 'Friction slows the ___' and 'Gravity pulls the apple ___'.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can transfer the vocabulary and the contact/non-contact split to examples they have not seen before, showing the words are owned rather than recalled for one picture.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE/vocabulary objective: the target is naming and correctly using force words and the contact/non-contact distinction, not calculating or explaining cause and effect.
Keep magnetism and gravity as separate non-contact forces; conflating them is a known difficulty. The deeper action-at-a-distance/field idea is developed later and is not the goal here.

Demonstrate magnetism as non-contact by showing a magnet attracting an object (e.g. a paperclip) across a gap, not by a magnet already stuck to a surface; the magnetic force acting without touching is the point.
Introduce 'weight' as a force (the pull of gravity) and keep it distinct from 'mass'; full mass/weight quantification comes later and should not be attempted at this age.

Sorting, matching, labelling and quiz-style tasks check whether vocabulary has stuck but do not by themselves provide the first-hand experience that anchors a word to a phenomenon; pair them with hands-on or richly depicted examples.

Address common intuitive errors explicitly: that gravity/magnetism need contact or a medium ('no gravity in space', gravity 'needs air'), that friction or gravity is just a 'thing' not a named force, that only pushes and pulls count as forces, and that water/air don't push (ignoring upthrust and air resistance).

At ages 5–7 forces vocabulary (push, pull) arises informally through play; in England's national curriculum, forces are first statutory in Year 3 (other UK nations' curricula differ). US NGSS K-PS2-1 covers push/pull strengths and directions but its assessment boundary excludes non-contact forces, so the contact/non-contact distinction goes beyond Kindergarten NGSS scope.

Concrete delivery can be low-tech (word wall, labelled images, picture/example-and-non-example cards, real objects to handle) or interactive; interactive reveal/drag mechanics are optional ways to stage the same learning, not requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing is made.

One source (Pine, Messer & St John 2001 / PSTT Common Misconceptions) is marked verified:false in the row; the specific misconceptions it supports (gravity/friction treated as phenomena not forces, 'no gravity in space') are retained as common patterns to watch for, not as verified findings.

The original entry rated a 3D environment and in-role dialogue as 'poor' fit with sweeping justifications; these have been softened — a 3D or conversational format is simply less efficient for anchoring precise vocabulary at this age, not incapable of teaching it. No universal 'only this teaches' claim is asserted.

The original row used a 'fridge magnet' as the non-contact magnetism exemplar and described it as a case where 'nothing is touching'. Because a fridge magnet is in contact with the fridge, this was corrected in every learner-facing occurrence to a magnet pulling a paperclip across a gap, matching the row's own assessment item and giving an accurate non-contact demonstration. A fridge magnet remains a valid everyday magnetism example, but is unsuitable for a 'nothing touching' demonstration.

The boat example ('a force pushing UP from the water' = upthrust, vs weight pulling down) is physically sound and retained. No arithmetic or force-direction errors were found requiring correction in learner-facing content.
Interactive reveal/zoom/drag examples from the original recommendation are preserved as optional concrete mechanisms, not mandated implementations.
Independent final review confirmed the fridge-magnet correction is applied consistently across every learner-facing occurrence and found no remaining contradictions or unsupported categorical claims.

probeDeeper: The magnet pulled the paperclip without touching it — was that a contact or a non-contact force? What about when I push a door?
You said the ball drops — what's the name of the force that pulls it down?
Show me something you can TWIST and something you can SQUASH. What force are you using?
A boat floats — there's a force pushing UP on it from the water. Do you know its name?
assess.correctAnswer: Squeezing a sponge = a squash (a push). The ball dropping = gravity (its weight pulling it down). The sledge slowing = friction. Stretching the band = a stretch (a pull). The magnet pulling the paperclip = a pull / a non-contact force (magnetism). Uses the specific term for each and can say which need touching (contact) and which don't (gravity, magnetism).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Everything is just a push' (or just 'a force') — one word for all of them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the specific word each time (squash, stretch, pull); build a word wall with a picture example for each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels squashing, stretching and gravity all as 'a push' or 'a force'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The ball just falls because it's heavy' — doesn't name gravity or weight.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name gravity as the pull of the Earth and weight as that pull; use it whenever something falls.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For the dropped ball, doesn't reach for 'gravity' or 'weight'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The sledge just stops on its own' — doesn't name friction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name friction as the rubbing force between surfaces that slows things down; use it for the grass, the brakes, the sledge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the slowing with no 'friction' word.

responseLevels.gap: Calls most things 'a push' or 'a force' with no specific words; doesn't name gravity or friction; can't tell contact from non-contact.
responseLevels.full: Names the specific force in each situation (squash, stretch, twist, gravity/weight, friction, air resistance, upthrust, magnetic pull) and sorts them into contact and non-contact — using the terms correctly in fresh scenarios.
responseLevels.partial: Uses several force words correctly for clear cases (push, pull, stretch) but reaches for a general word in others, or names gravity/friction only when prompted — a growing vocabulary, not yet reliable across examples.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Let's play a describing game. I'll show you things happening and you tell me what FORCE is at work each time, using the best word: I squeeze a sponge... I let go of a ball and it drops... a sledge slows down on the grass... I stretch an elastic band... a magnet pulls a paperclip across the table. What's happening in each one?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: About USE in context, not definitions. A child who owns the words picks the specific term for each situation (squash, gravity, friction, stretch, non-contact pull) rather than calling everything 'a push' or 'a force'. Listen for whether they use gravity/weight for the falling ball and tag the magnet as non-contact. Vague 'it just falls / it stops', or one word for everything, reveals the gap.
